case_name: FTC v. Cox Media Group, MindSift, 1010 Digital Works
claims_made: Smart devices capture real-time intent data by listening to consumer conversations
Voice data is paired with behavioral data to target in-market consumers
Advertisers get access to 'Active Listening' intent signals from device microphones
The service uses AI to process ambient audio for advertising purposes
reality: NO microphone data was collected or used by the service
Service relied entirely on standard ad-targeting techniques
Targeting used cookies, behavioral browsing data, and demographic profiling
'Active Listening' was a deceptive marketing label, not a real technology
Ads were also not accurately placed in customers' desired geographic locations

timeline.event: CMG pitch deck surfaces publicly claiming 'active listening' via smart devices
Security researchers and journalists analyze claims; hypothesize standard ad targeting rebranded
FTC announces settlement confirming service never used voice data

compliance_lessons: Technical claims in sales materials must match actual system capabilities
Aspirational language implying unbuilt functionality constitutes deceptive trade practices
FTC actively enforces against misleading AI capability claims under Section 5
Consumer fear of 'phones listening' is widespread but targeting comes from behavioral data, not microphones
Audit pitch decks and marketing collateral for regulatory compliance before distribution
